Three reviewers on Fable, one per row, each in its own clone. All three found the same two classes again: the eval runner removing a folder it had not made, and slow reading of a crafted line. That is two rounds running for each; the brief's rule stops the work at a third. And a folder made between the check and `git worktree add` was deleted, since the folder joined `live` first (security F2, CONFIRMED). Now an existing folder of any kind stops the case with the command to remove it by hand, a folder joins `live` only after `git worktree add` made it, the add runs without `--force`, and two cases with one id stop the run.
- `code()` was still quadratic on a quote and many escaped quotes (80,000: 38.7 s), and so was the comment strip on a line ending in CR (security F4, F5; regression 4; CONFIRMED). It is now one pass from left to right; a test times 80,000 of each.

Calls are read on the raw line again, and the shorthand is back except in a destructuring line. Block comments are taken out of the code now.
- The breaker regex was quadratic on a run of blanks (security F6, regression 4; CONFIRMED), and missed `**Regression-of**:`, `_.._`, a task box and a blank before the colon; "10, 11" named 10 only (docs W3, regression 6). The separators now each end at a comma or a `#`, and those forms count.
- `sections()` took a fence line inside an HTML comment as a fence: it failed open for two hidden comments holding fence lines and closed for a complete body after one (docs W4, regression 1; CONFIRMED). Comments are now tracked line by line, in linear time.
- Tests the regression reviewer's mutations showed missing: a fence closed by the other kind, by a line with an info string, or by a shorter fence before the headings; a key form inside a string; a call named in a comment.
- Docs: the comments and notes that overstated round 2 are corrected above and in the code.

Repro (Fable's probe, not kept): write `.jbmem.lock` as `pid <own pid> host <os.hostname()> since <iso> token aaaa`, make `Date.now` add 61000 after its third call, call `withLock(dir, () => 'GOT', { waitMs: 600 })`, then look for `token aaaa` in the file.
    - Fixed (`store.js`, both copies): `clockMoved()` compares `Date.now()` with `performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()`, the wall clock at the process's start plus the monotonic time since (within 2 ms on this PC: `la-offset.out` in the notes folder `rs-t-lockagestep/`; up to 1.8 ms in six processes, CONFIRMED by Opus in round 1, not re-run). Past 1 s the clock has moved, and `lockBreakable` takes a lock's age as at most the time this `withLock` has watched that same lock text, on the monotonic clock (`tryBreakLock` keeps the text and when it was first seen). The 60 s, 30 s and 5 s rules are unchanged otherwise. A `.break` file is not removed for its age once the clock moved (one that is not a plain file still is). With the clock unmoved nothing changes: a lock left by a crash is broken as before (a dead pid's once it is 5 s old).
    - Why not always watch: `updateState` waits 2 s, so a rule that made every waiter watch a lock for 5 s would leave hooks unable to clear a crashed lock. In a process whose clock moved, a wait now ends with `JBMEM_LOCKED`; the next command, its clock unmoved, breaks a lock that is really left behind. Not covered: a clock moved before the waiting process started, while a holder is mid-job (that waiter sees no move; the holder's milliseconds are the window). Also not covered, RS-T-lockagewin (left only for a lock without a trusted stamp since RS-T-lockagemono, below; INFERRED by Fable from V8's source in round 1, not run, since a run needs the system clock set; that Node's `Date.now` goes through that V8 class is HYPOTHESIZED by Fable): on Windows V8 re-reads the system time only after a minute or a step back, so a waiter that started before a forward step may not see it and can still break a live holder's lock; a step back is seen at once.

Where two processes with one host name and platform read different monotonic clocks (a time namespace, WSL1 and WSL2 on one folder, two machines), the stamp is from another clock: a waiter ahead gets the mtime's age, the lower one, and a waiter behind by D reads the stamp as D younger: a lock whose true age is at least D is kept until its true age is D plus 60 s (D plus 5 s for a holder that is gone), whatever D is, and a younger one has a stamp ahead of now, not trusted, and is aged by its file time as before (INFERRED from `monoAge` and `lockBreakable`; the file time half CONFIRMED by Sonnet by a probe in review round 3 with D of 30 s and 100 s, a live pid and a 61 s mtime, not re-run here). The proposed fix was `node --test --test-timeout` on the three test steps. Probes, data and scripts are in `rs-t-hang75/` of the sessions' notes folder (the probes in `rs-t-hang75/probe/`); each was read before it ran, and those that make folders or processes remove them (`removed`, `copy removed` and `kill signals delivered` lines in their output).

- What `--test-timeout` can end (CONFIRMED):
  - In Node's test runner `runTestFile` builds the file-level test with `{ __proto__: null, signal: opts.signal }` only (`lib/internal/test_runner/runner.js` line 364 on branch v22.x, 507 on v24.x, 558 on v26.x, read with `gh api` on 2026-11-17; `probe/node-source-fetch.sh`, `probe/node-source-fileopts.out`). On v24.x and v26.x that test's timeout is then set to null (`runner.js` line 284 on v24.x, 307 on v26.x), so it gets none. On v22.x it is not: every subtest copies its parent's timeout (`lib/internal/test_runner/test.js` line 554), and the root carries `--test-timeout` (`runner.js` line 663), so each test file as a whole gets the limit. This bullet first said no branch gave the file a timeout, read from `runTestFile` alone; review round 1 found it (below). On every branch the limit runs on the test file's own thread, so a test blocked synchronously is not ended by it.
  - Probe (`probe/hang.test.js`, `probe/run.sh`, `probe/all.sh`; Windows, Node 26.13.1, `--test-timeout=5000`, an outer `timeout` of 40 s or 60 s as the guard; `probe/all-win26.out`, `probe/configC-win26.out`): a test waiting on a promise with a timer open was named ("test timed out after 5000ms"), but the run went on to the guard; with `--test-force-exit` added it ended after 6 s, exit 1, the test named. A busy loop, and a `spawnSync` with no `timeout` of a child that never ends, ran to the guard. A `spawnSync` with no `timeout` of a child that exits at once and leaves a detached grandchild holding its stdout also ran to the guard, and the grandchild was still running after the guard stopped the run. With `timeout: 5000` on the `spawnSync` itself, the never-ending child was stopped after 5 s (status null, SIGTERM, ETIMEDOUT), and the grandchild case returned after 5 s with status 0 and ETIMEDOUT, so a test that checks only `status` passes it.
  - Not run on this PC: Node 22 and 24 (not installed; getting them is a download) and macOS. The self-check below runs on all 9 CI jobs. On ddfd0a9 it gave 2 of 6 on the three Node 22.23.5 jobs, each hung case ended at about 3 s as a failure of the file, not of the case, and 6 of 6 on the six Node 24 and 26 jobs (run 44198765849, the job logs read here).
- What was built: `.github/run-tests.sh` runs node --test for each of the three test steps; `dev/check-workflow-timeouts.js` refuses the word `timeout` on a `run:` line, so the flag can't sit in `tests.yml`. Each step sets `TRAILMARK_TEST_LIMIT_MS` for its system and `TRAILMARK_TEST_LIMITS`. In `enforce` mode the wrapper adds `--test-timeout` (on Node 24 and later only, since round 1), `--test-force-exit` and `--require ./.github/test-limits.js`, a preload that gives each `spawnSync`, `execFileSync` and `execSync` call with no timeout of its own (no `timeout` key, or 0, null or undefined, which Node reads as none; the key alone at first; since round 2 any other timeout, one Node refuses included, goes to Node as the call gave it) the same limit, stops the child with SIGKILL unless the call names its own `killSignal` (since round 1), and, when it fires, throws an error that names the call, the limit and the test file's line; the file also exits 1 when a test swallowed that error, and `tap-annotate.js` names each stopped call in an error annotation (since round 1). The preload acts only in a test file's process (`NODE_TEST_CONTEXT`), not in node --test's own. In `report` mode node --test runs with the same arguments as before this change, and the wrapper runs under `set -euo pipefail`, as the step's own shell did: with a `tap-annotate.js` that throws, a passing run exits 1 with that line and 0 with `set -u` alone (`probe/sete-check.sh`, run on a copy before the commit; it also gave 0 for the `pass` and `own` cases and 1, with two error annotations, for a planted failure).
- `--test-force-exit` also lets a file whose tests all passed exit with a child or a timer still open, where before such a file kept its step waiting (`probe/leak.test.js`: exit 0 with `ProcessWrap` and `Timeout` listed at exit). In enforce mode this loosens what the step judges (PLAYBOOK "Reviewing" step 7), so the preload writes the file and what is open at exit, and `.github/tap-annotate.js` turns that line into a warning.
- The self-check, `.github/test-limits-check.js` (a new step, "Test limits check (reports only)", `continue-on-error: true`, 3 min limit): it runs `run-tests.sh` in enforce mode with a 3 s limit on `.github/test-limits-fixture.js`, one case at a time under a guard of its own (60 s at first; since round 1, 25 s, with a budget of 150 s for the whole check, 160 s since round 2, so that its result and its cleanup come within the 3 min step limit; on Node 22 it skips `async` and says why). `pass` and `own` (a call with its own timeout) must pass; `async`, `spawnsync` and `orphan` (the grandchild case, through `execFileSync`) must fail and name the case; `swallowed` must pass its test and fail its file. 6 of 6 on Windows and in WSL Ubuntu, Node 26.13.1 both (`probe/wsl-check.out`). Mutations (`probe/mutate.js`, `probe/mutate2-win26.out`, Windows): each of 10 takes one part away (each of the wrapper's three flags, enforce mode itself, the `spawnSync` and the `execFileSync` throw, the exit code, the limit, the own-timeout rule, the test-file rule), and each is caught (10 lines "applied in", 10 "caught"), with the unchanged control at 6 of 6. The `execSync` wrapper has no case in the self-check; the scratch probe's `execsync` mode showed it stopped and named (`probe/run2-win26.out`). A guarded run first left its `node --test` processes and folder behind (`probe/mutate-win26.out`), since the guard stops only `bash`; the fixture now writes its own pid, and the second run left none (`probe/leftovers.ps1`, "found 0").
- Sizing (from data): `steptimes.sh` read every job of the `tests.yml` runs GitHub listed into `steps.tsv` (rows for 296 runs and 2,739 jobs, steps started 2026-11-04 03:52Z to 2026-11-17 21:53Z, and the three lines of the "Server Error" body of the one request that failed; first written as 297 runs and 2,742 jobs, counting those lines; the slowest times are not changed by them); `summary.out` gives each step's slowest passing time. "Checks added in 0.4.5": 173 s Linux, 335 s macOS, 748 s Windows; "trailmark tests": 203, 295 and 447 s; "trailmark-codex tests": 193, 252 and 406 s. CI keeps no per-test times (the TAP goes to a file), so the slowest test comes from one local run of every test (`release-check.sh --only '.'` on e0dea5f, 17:09 to 17:31 local, under load from the probes): 153.0 s, "0.6.0 commit folders: a folder that joins the session's commit folders is swept ..." (`local-slowest-tests.out`). Limits: 240 s Linux, 300 s macOS, 400 s Windows, 1.6, 2.0 and 2.6 times that test. A limit at least the slowest passing step (748 s on Windows) would not fit: with every step at its slowest passing time and the check step at its limit, the Windows job, with one hang in that step spending the 748 s limit, would take 1,877 + 748 + 180 = 2,805 s against its 2,700 s limit (`nest-check.out` gives the 1,877 s). - "Pushing and CI" step 3: the three test steps run in `report` mode, so nothing that passed before can fail in them. `tap-annotate.js` adds a notice with each step's five slowest tests and a warning naming each test over the limit, which gives CI's own per-test times. The self-check step reports only. Enforcing is the follow-up item RS-T-hang75-enforce below (all of this as built in PR #82, until RS-T-hang75-enforce). The new `tap-annotate.js` lines, on the local run's TAP with a 100 s limit, listed the same 738 tests and the same 153.0 s test as `slowest-tests.js`, and warned for that test only; with no limit set they warned for none.

So a limit there would meet load first.
- Not covered: a test blocked in its own JavaScript (a busy loop) is ended by no limit inside node. On Node 22 a test that waits on something asynchronous is ended by no limit in enforce mode either, since `run-tests.sh` gives `--test-timeout` only on Node 24 and later (round 1; until RS-T-hang75-enforce, PR #84, whose preload gives each `test()` call the limit on Node 22). A test that passes while a detached grandchild holds the test file's own stdout leaves node --test waiting, with every test `ok` and none named (CONFIRMED by the round 1 reviewer, row `n-inherit` of `r1-repro/p2-neighbors-win26.out`, not re-run here). - The probe (`run-probe2.sh`, `patch-probe2.js`, `probe-steps2.js`; a patched clone prints, for each session start, its wall time split into parts, CONFIRMED by its lines): pre (from the spawn call to Node's `performance.timeOrigin`), load (from `timeOrigin` to the launcher's old `T0 = Date.now()` line, after its first modules), work (the launcher's git work), script (the sandboxed script, with any time past its timeout before the kill took), and after (from the script's end to the exit). Beside each run, 20 bare `node -e 0` spawns under the same load give pre and after outside the launcher.
- What reproduced it: 16 busy loops (one per core) did not (`probe2-1.out`, 0 of 20 past 10 s, longest 8,686 ms). 48 loops did (`probe2-2.out`, 15:30 to 15:36, load 100%, 81 node processes): 8 of 20 starts past 10 s, 3 stopped by the launcher, the longest 12,874 ms. In those 20, pre was 323 to 1,917 ms, load 402 to 2,451 ms, work 4,087 to 5,708 ms, script 1,543 to 4,802 ms and after 14 to 948 ms. The bare spawns took up to 3,236 ms, and up to 2,190 ms before `timeOrigin` (maxima over the bare-spawn lines under the loops, computed after a first reading took the last line). Lesson: "The busy loops that reproduced a load failure the day before did not reproduce it".
- The cause (CONFIRMED by those lines): no one step. Under load every part grows, and the launcher's limits counted from its old `T0`, after load, while the host's 10 s counts from the spawn. The 4,687 ms of RS-T-startstopped was load in this sense (`T0` measured from `timeOrigin` by `performance.now()`).

- The fix (3eb9e73, both copies of `scripts/trailmark.js`): `const T0 = Math.floor(performance.timeOrigin);`, so the script's limit `max(300, 9000 - spent)` (4500 for commit-start) and the git work's 5 s (`started = T0` in `hookMode`) count from the process's start. With `JBMEM_SHOW_CLOCK=1` the launcher prints the script's spent and timeout, and both clocks as times (4938218); without it nothing changes (CONFIRMED by both round 2 reviewers, not re-run).
- Clock agreement (`clock-agree.js`, 40 runs each, CONFIRMED): a child's `Math.floor(performance.timeOrigin)` came 13 to 22 ms after the parent's spawn call on Linux (WSL, Node 18) and 28 to 49 ms after on Windows (Node 26). macOS and Node 20, 22 and 24 were not run here; CI's 9 jobs run the new test.
- The comparison (`alternate.sh`, P F F P: parent 692e8ff and fix 3eb9e73 under 48 loops, 8 loaded starts a run, 15:41 to 15:58, `alt-*.out`; counted by `lost.js`, CONFIRMED): 16 loaded starts each. Parent: 9 lost (4 stopped by the launcher, 5 past 10 s with no stop, where the host stops the hook), longest 15,155 ms. Fix: 9 lost, all 9 stopped by the launcher, longest 11,766 ms. So the fix makes each lost start the launcher's own stop and cuts the longest overrun; it does not save a handoff under this load. Lesson: "A time fix cut the longest overrun and left the lost handoffs as they were".
- The test (`hook clock: the time before the launcher's first line counts against the git work and the script`, both copies of `handoff-checks.test.js`): a preload holds the process 3,600 ms after `timeOrigin` and before the launcher's first line. Each clock must lie between the test's spawn call and the hold's start (50 ms either way), each time spent must be at least the hold and at most the time from its clock to the end of the spawn, the script's timeout must follow the rule, and git must get no time for the commits since the handoff.

## Verification guidance from the Claude Code team (2026-11-16, branch `claude/verification-guidance` off 6ac3074)

The user asked to add the testing guidance of the post "How the Claude Code team thinks about verification" (claude.dev blog; its date was not settled: one fetch reported 2026-11-16, another showed none) to this project. The post was read through a fetch on 2026-11-16 (HTTP 200, no redirect). Each of its practices was set beside `PLAYBOOK.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `LESSONS.md`. Of the instruction files, only `PLAYBOOK.md` changed; `CLAUDE.md` and "Do not attempt" were left alone, since a change there is asked first.

Added to `PLAYBOOK.md`, each new:

- "Testing" step 18: a change to a hook or a skill is also run in a real host session (Claude Code, or Codex for the Codex copy) before its PR, and the notes say how the copy was loaded and what the session showed. A PR whose host run is still untested is not set to auto-merge until the user decides. The post ranks a run of the real thing above tests, and end-to-end tests above unit tests.
- "Testing" step 19: an invariant test for a function that folds, normalizes, parses or encodes text from outside, over inputs a loop generates from a stated alphabet and length range. No property-test library, since adding one is a download.
- "Testing" step 20: a rewrite that must keep behavior compares old and new code over the same inputs, with intended differences listed. "Writing" step 18 and RS-T-ziptz already did this for one case each.
- "Testing" step 21: no sleep, rerun in place of a cause, new skip or looser bound for a failing test without a proven cause. The two existing kinds of skip (on a time sign, step 7; on a system where the test can't run) are named as allowed.
- "Committing" step 7: a `Verified:` line in each commit made in a session, `Verified: none` with the reason included.
- "Pushing and CI" step 3: a new check that can fail CI or stop a commit reports only for at least one PR first, as the watchdog test step in `tests.yml` does (`continue-on-error: true`, read on 6ac3074).
- "Reviewing" step 7: a change that edits a check that judges it names that check, and the reviewer runs the base branch's version too where it can.
- "Reviewing" step 8: a fix whose own test or check still fails after three attempts at that same failure goes to the user before a fourth, with auto-merge off. Review rounds that find something new are not counted.

Already covered here, so not added: no "flaky" label ("Do not attempt"); one reviewer for each row, with rounds that build on the rounds before ("Reviewing" steps 1 and 2); a review only at a fixed head (step 2's detached clone, step 5's held pushes); cheap checks before a push (`--only`, then `--sums --quick`); a miss turned into a rule once it is seen twice (the lessons check, step 7); pruning (`CLAUDE.md`: keep `PLAYBOOK.md` short).

Not taken, for the user:

- The post deletes a test whose cause can't be found and writes down why. That conflicts with this project's rule that a failure gets a proven cause, so it is left out.
- A "verify" skill in `.claude/skills/` that starts a host session with the changed copy and checks the handoff. "Testing" step 18 asks for the run but has no such tool yet. Building one is a separate piece of work.
- Scoring reviewers against past reverts and incidents, and a checklist keyed by triggers read from a diff: there is no such corpus here yet. `dev/lessons.sh <words>` is the nearest form of the checklist.
- A property-test library (fast-check): a download.

Checks on this change: `dev/lessons.sh --check` and the dash scan (results in each commit message of this branch). Docs review round 1 (Sonnet, on 6ac3074..a64c6d4): no WRONG, five COULD BE CLEARER, all fixed in 77b0e54 after a check of each here: step 18 now says a PR untested in a host is not set to auto-merge until the user decides; step 21 names step 5's reruns; "Committing" step 7 is scoped to commits made in a session, since 7 of the 30 commit subjects up to 6ac3074 are GitHub merge commits, which a `Verified:` line can't reach; "Reviewing" step 8 counts attempts at the same failure, not review rounds; and this section's first lines now say "Of the instruction files" before "only `PLAYBOOK.md` changed", and say the post's date was not settled instead of stating one. Docs review round 2 (Sonnet, on a64c6d4..77b0e54): no WRONG, and two COULD BE CLEARER points on this paragraph's wording (name 77b0e54 in place of "the next commit" and put the merge-commit count by the "Committing" step 7 item; say what the fix of this section's first lines changed; the round's report is in the coordinator session's transcript, not in a file), fixed in the notes after PR #78 (branch `claude/notes-after-pr78`).

## Next version: the pause watch (2026-11-15, branch `claude/upbeat-bouman-62d581` off 79d0715)

New scope, asked by the coordinating session (session 5685aa10) on the user's report that "pause for reboot" got no checkpoint: not a deferred item, so the deferred-item rule of `CLAUDE.md` does not cover it, and a push or PR is asked of the user. Design and reasons: `dev/pause-watch-design.md`.

- What it does: a second UserPromptSubmit hook, `trailmark.js --hook pause-watch`. The launcher reads the prompt in `lib/pausewords.js` before it loads the rest of its code; on a match it finds the memory folder and starts `hook-pause-watch.js` with one word from a fixed list. The hook asks Claude to run `trailmark:checkpoint` before the turn ends, or to ignore the note when the word was about something else. Silent for a repo not set up, a subagent, `"pauseWatch": {"on": false}`, and when this session wrote the handoff within `hints.freshCheckpointMinutes`. It writes nothing. Claude Code copy only.

## Next version: RS-D-jobtimeout (2026-11-15, branch `claude/rs-d-jobtimeout` off 79d0715)

Worked under the user's delegation of 2026-11-11 for the deferred items. The item is dev tooling: `tests.yml` set no `timeout-minutes`, so a job that hangs held a PR for GitHub's default of 6 hours, and a macOS job hung twice in the step "trailmark tests" with no log (PR #50, section "Next version: RS-A-firstcheck"; PR #63's head fa6134a, section "Next version: RS-A-linkgit, RS-A-relpath and RS-A-bytepath"); the data below hold a third macOS job that ran 6 h 5 min with no step reported and ended `cancelled` (run 42450240343, found in review round 2; INFERRED to be a hang ended by GitHub's 6 hours, see the bullet on what the limits change). No shipped code and no shipped doc changes. `tests.yml` is listed in `SHA256SUMS`, which `--sums` regenerated. The scripts and outputs named here are in `rs-d-jobtimeout-scripts/` in the sessions' shared notes folder.

- The data, CONFIRMED here from the Actions API (read-only `gh api` calls; times UTC, 2026-11-15). The limits are sized from `node job-durations-all.js durations-all.tsv` (20:19:16Z to 20:26:31Z, `durations-all.out`): every listed run of `tests.yml`, 332 of any status and event (253 passed, 52 failed, 25 cancelled, 2 still going and not read), and every attempt of each (`jobs?filter=all`): 2,965 job rows, from 328 of the 330 completed runs (`worst-case.js` counts the runs with a row; the other 2 gave none). A job counts when its own conclusion is success (2,575 jobs), and a step when its own is, also inside a run that failed. A job's time is its `started_at` to `completed_at`, which leaves out the wait for a runner. The slowest passing job and step on each system, and each limit's ratio to it, printed by `worst-case.js` (`worst-case-1.out`):

  | macOS | 11.53 (Node 22, run 43542640756, c858dcb) | 25, 2.17 | 5.37, limit 12, 2.24 | 5.03, limit 12, 2.38 | 4.20, limit 12, 2.86 |

- Why these numbers. One limit for every job would have to be about 45 for Windows, which leaves a macOS hang running 45 min where its slowest passing job took 11.5; the old idea of about 20 min would have cancelled Windows jobs that passed in 21.5. The step limits are per system so that each fires before its job's limit: for a hang in any one test step, with every other step at its slowest passing time and all the job's other time (at most 4.08 min on Windows, 2.25 on macOS, 2.98 on Linux) put before it, the step's limit ends it and the steps after it are done inside the job's limit (that they run at all after a step failed rests on their `if: always()`, and what GitHub does then is HYPOTHESIZED, bullet "What GitHub does at a limit"; `worst-case-1.out`; the tightest is a hang in "trailmark-codex tests" on macOS, ended at 24.65 of 25 minutes). Round 1 found that a single step limit of 25 for the 0.4.5 step could never fire before the job's 20 or 25 on Linux and macOS. On macOS, where both hangs were, a hang in "trailmark tests" is stopped by 19.62 minutes into the job at worst. The two hangs were cancelled by hand, and their jobs closed 44 min 37 s and 31 min 39 s into the step (on fa6134a the cancel itself came 26 min 39 s in). That step's time has grown: the 0.4.5 step took under 1 min in 277 of the 1,686 jobs of the 100 + 100 data, the newest in run 42926020989 (created 2026-11-10T23:45:55Z, `gh api`), and up to 12.47 min since; INFERRED that it grew with the tests added to `handoff-checks.test.js`. When a passing job or step comes within about two thirds of its limit, the limits are raised in a PR of their own, and `worst-case.js` is run again with them. Nothing runs that watch yet: review round 2 found the Windows 0.4.5 step's daily maximum rising from 4.08 min (2026-11-08) to 12.47 (2026-11-15), so it is the deferred item RS-D-limitwatch below.
- What GitHub does at a limit, read from its docs by a web-fetch subagent (the workflow-syntax page reached it as a summary, the contexts table and the limits page word for word; not re-read here). `jobs.<id>.timeout-minutes` and a step's `timeout-minutes` may both use the `matrix` context (table "Context availability"); the job is cancelled when its limit runs out, and a step's process is killed at its own. The docs do not say whether a step that runs out fails, whether later `if: always()` steps still run, or the job's conclusion: HYPOTHESIZED that a step that runs out fails, the steps after it with `if: always()` run, and its log is kept, as for any failed step, until a run shows it. Whether the wait for a runner counts against the job limit: the docs speak of execution time only, INFERRED that it does not. That GitHub takes the expressions at all is CONFIRMED only by a run: 94d0782's job expression was accepted, and its 9 jobs started (see below).
- What the limits change for a hang like the two seen, INFERRED from those records and not tried (no hang can be made to order). A step that hangs while its runner still answers is killed at the step's limit, and that job then has a log, which tells a hung test from a runner that stopped. A runner that stopped answering cannot kill its step, so only the job's limit is left. INFERRED from one manual cancel: on fa6134a, GitHub closed the job as cancelled 5 min after the cancel (22:02:33Z after 21:57:33Z), and the job left no log, which fits a runner that had stopped answering (the older section's own INFERRED). If a job limit is enforced the same way, the PR waits at most the job's limit and about 5 min more. It reads each `.github/workflows/*.yml` and `*.yaml` line by line and fails when a job, a key one level below the top-level `jobs:`, has no `timeout-minutes` one level below it; a step's limit does not count for its job. It also fails on a `timeout-minutes` value, of a job or a step (since round 2 also one written as a step's first key, after `- `), that is not a whole number from 1 to 360 or an expression of one shape: `matrix.os == '<label>' && <n> || ... || <n>`, each `<n>` a whole number from 1 to 360. Round 1 added the rule that the last part is a number, so that no matrix row falls through to `false`; round 2 made the rest of the shape strict, which refuses a hex, exponent or negative number, a bare context, a function and parentheses. What it guards against, since batch 5: a limit that is missing or malformed in the plain YAML the workflows use. It does not guard against a limit hidden on purpose: the workflows are written in this repo, so hiding one takes a commit that review sees, and a real YAML parser would be needed to catch it (deferred as RS-D-yamlparse). Since batch 4 (rounds 3 and 4 each found YAML forms the rules of the round before missed, PLAYBOOK "Reviewing" step 6), the check reads only that plain YAML: it accepts a limit in one shape only, `timeout-minutes: <value>` indented with spaces, as a key or as a step's first key after `- `, with a space or a tab before any end-of-line comment, and refuses the rest. That is any line, except a full-line comment, that holds `timeout` or `minutes` in any case outside that shape (a quoted, capitalised or anchored key, a space before the colon or none after it, a `run:` or `name:` line holding the word); any line with a character outside ASCII, comments too (a no-break space, a look-alike letter); a double-quoted key that holds an escape (`"timeout\x2dminutes"` is the same key to YAML); an explicit `? ` key; and a flow mapping as a step or as a key's value (`- {...}`, `env: {...}`, not `${{ }}`). Both workflows are ASCII only, hold the two words only on their limit lines and in full-line comments, and have no flow mapping, so neither is refused (`grep`, and the check's run on them). Valid workflows can be refused, on the safe side: a `run:` line, a line of a `run: |` block or a `name:` that holds either word, a comment with a non-ASCII letter, an `env: {...}`. Since batch 5, outside a block scalar (`run: |`, `run: >`), it also refuses an anchor or an alias, any flow mapping, a flow sequence other than a one-line list of plain words (the matrix's `[ubuntu-latest, ...]` and `['22', '24', '26']`, `branches: [main]`), and a line that is neither a key with its colon nor a `- ` list item (a key whose colon is on the next line, or a deeper line with no `: ` and no leading `- `, which round 6 showed is not every value that runs on); inside a block scalar only the word and ASCII rules apply, since its lines are script text. Since batch 6 (round 6): an anchor or an alias is an `&` or a `*` that starts a node (after the indent, after `- ` or `? `, or after `: `), whatever follows it, so `&&k` and `*&k` are refused, and an `&` or a `*` inside a plain value (`a && b`, `ls *.js`) passes, as YAML reads it; a quote starts a quoted scalar only where a node starts, so a quote inside a plain key (`x'y: &k`) no longer hides what follows it; a `${{ }}` that holds `: ` or ` #` is read as it is; and outside a block scalar, a line deeper than a key or a list item with a value on its own line is refused, unless it is blank or a full-line comment, which the check skips before this rule (since batch 7, round 7: before, this sentence said "whatever the line holds"). The one-line list is read on the line as written: plain words or quoted plain words. Neither workflow holds any of these outside its block scalars (the check's run on them). A `#` counts as a comment only after a space or a tab, as in YAML, so `30#c` is read whole and refused. What the limits change for it, INFERRED from GitHub's auto-merge rules and not tried here: a job that runs out of time ends as failed or cancelled, not as passed, so auto-merge cannot merge on it, as before. But a session no longer has to notice the hang to cancel it. And if auto-merge is left on while the job is rerun from the Actions page, one passing rerun merges the PR at once, with no second or third rerun. So under the three-reruns rule, auto-merge still has to be taken off before the first rerun. Under the fresh-head rule, the job ends at its limit, and the session pushes the fresh head and sets auto-merge again as before, with no cancel. A step limit that fires leaves a log that shows the step ran out of time, but not which test hung: `tap-annotate.js` runs inside the same step, after `node --test`, so it never runs, and no step uploads the TAP files (round 2, INFERRED from `tests.yml`; deferred as RS-D-killedsteplog). ## Next version: RS-A-casefoldfs (2026-11-14, branch `claude/rs-a-casefoldfs` off a8ad9cc)

Worked under the user's go-ahead of 2026-11-10 for the deferred items and "continue with RS-A-casefoldfs" of 2026-11-14 (relayed by the session that started this one). The item was flagged in the section below: status is read where it should not be. The code, the tests and the sentences in SECURITY.md are commit 3fa192c, and the batch after review round 1 is commit e8a79e9, the one after round 2 commit 1b36285, the one after round 3 commit cdd67ed. Times are local, 2026-11-14. The probes, runners and outputs named here are in `rs-a-casefoldfs-scripts/` in the sessions' shared notes folder.

- Reproduced on 2246165 (CONFIRMED here, WSL, node 18.19.1, git 2.56.1, uid 1000, 19:57; `run-probe-2.sh` runs `probe-casefold-2.js`; `probe-2-parent-1.out`; both plugin copies answer the same; a8ad9cc has the same library files, PR #64 changed instruction files only). On a Windows drive (`/mnt/e`, which folds case), with `dir/a`, `dir/b` and `dir/F` tracked and a repo on disk at `dir/f`: `lstat dir/F` finds a folder. With a config in `dir/f/.git` that includes a share's text, status is read (three lines, `AD dir/F`). With that config broken, `git status` exits 128 with "bad config line 1 in file <base>/dir/F/.git/config", so git opens it. With two tracked names (`dir/a`, `dir/F`) and with one, the check answers `submodule-pointer` (the section below had this "by the security reviewer, not re-run"). The control on ext4 (/tmp, keeps case): `lstat dir/F` is ENOENT, `git status` exits 0 with the broken config, and status is read with three, two and one names. A share's text is a local path on Linux: nothing left the machine and nothing ran.
- The cause, in `farWorktree` (`gitfacts.js`). A tracked file whose path is now a folder with a `.git` is checked like a submodule, since `git status` looks for a repo there. One or two tracked names in a folder are each looked up with `lstat`, so the file system answers as it will for git. Three or more: the folder is listed, and outside Windows and macOS only a subfolder whose listed name equals a tracked name as text was checked. The listing holds `f`, the tracked name is `F`, and git's lookup of `F` finds `f`.
- The rule. Ask the file system by the tracked name, as git does: each tracked name that the listing does not hold is looked up, and one found as a folder is checked under the tracked name. This holds for any way a file system matches names, not only for case. The other ideas, and what each misses. Folding names in JavaScript: the code's own comment says lower case there does not match what Windows and macOS do (final sigma, Unicode forms), and a Linux mount can match in still other ways. Checking every subfolder on every system, the Windows and macOS way: it would refuse status on Linux for a repo next to tracked files whose `.git` leads away and that git never opens, which is an answer that changes for repos where nothing is wrong (INFERRED from the code, not run).
- The fix, both copies of `gitfacts.js`. In the branch that lists a folder, outside Windows and macOS and where the listing holds a subfolder (a name can only be found as a folder where there is one): each tracked name not in the listing is looked up with `fs.lstatSync(one, { throwIfNoEntry: false })`. A failure that is not "not there" (`notThere`) answers `unreadable-path`, as for one or two names. The time is looked at before each lookup (`git-timeout` under 0.8 s). `farWorktree` has a third argument `caseless`, by default `CASELESS`; its one caller in `scripts/` (`gitfacts.js:103`) passes two arguments, and only the tests pass the third. Windows and macOS: every subfolder is checked, as before.
- With the fix (`probe-2-fix-2.out`, 20:55, the files as committed; CONFIRMED here): the shape with three names and a share's text answers `submodule-pointer` in both copies, where 2246165's files read status. ## Next version: RS-A-linkgit, RS-A-relpath and RS-A-bytepath (2026-11-14, branch `claude/rs-a-linkgit` off a1c7269)

Worked under the user's go-ahead of 2026-11-10 for the deferred items. The three were flagged in the section below and share one cause: in `scripts/lib/gitbin.js` and `gitfacts.js` a lookup that fails for another reason than "not there" was read as "not there". The check then answered `''` and git ran, while git reached the same thing through a link or a relative path. The code, tests and shipped docs are commit 1e7b064. Times are local, 2026-11-14. The probes, runners and outputs named here are copied to `rs-a-linkgit-scripts/` in the sessions' shared notes folder, next to the working notes `rs-a-linkgit-notes.md`.

- Reproduced on a1c7269 (CONFIRMED here, WSL, node 18.19.1, git 2.56.1, 10:06 and 10:07; `wsl-repro.sh` runs `probe-linkgit.js`, `probe-relpath.js` and `probe-bytepath.js` on a copy under /tmp and removes it; outputs `repro-main-1.out`, `repro-main-2.out`). RS-A-linkgit: a `.git` that is a symlink to a gitdir whose config includes `//evil.invalid/share/x`. With the gitdir's real path at 300 bytes the check answers `network-config`. At 4,096 and at 4,097 bytes it answers `''` and the git facts are read (branch, head, status), and `git config user.name` in that folder answers through the link. With a filter in that config the marker file was not made at any of the three lengths; with a worktree in it status was `outside-worktree` at all three. RS-A-relpath: a submodule entry at a tracked path of 4,080 bytes whose `.git` file names `//evil.invalid/share/x/.git`. At a short path: `submodule-pointer`. At the long one Node fails by the whole path (4,126 bytes, ENAMETOOLONG), `farWorktree` answers `''`, and `git status --porcelain` reads that `.git` file (exit 128, "gitfile does not point to a valid repository"). RS-A-bytepath, with the reviewer's numbers (the top with its slash 182 bytes, 20 names of 100 two-byte letters): a folder in `.git/x` at 2,208 characters and 4,208 bytes that holds a link with the text `//evil.invalid/share/x` answers `''`, and `linked-gitdir` at a short path. New here, the same in ASCII: `long-path` at 4,129 and at 4,097 characters; `''` at exactly 4,096 (Linux opens 4,095 bytes at most, and the cap lets 4,096 through); `''` at 4,095 too (the folder lists, the link in it is at 4,097 bytes, and `localPath` took its failed lstat as "not there"); `linked-gitdir` at 4,090.
- What git does there (CONFIRMED here, the same run; the section below had "Git was not run on it" for RS-A-bytepath). The same folders under `.git/refs/heads`, with the link leading to a local file that holds HEAD's id: `git for-each-ref` from the top lists the ref through the link in each shape tried (two-byte names at 4,035 bytes from the top; ASCII at 4,129, 4,097, 4,096, 4,095 and 4,090 characters by the whole path). So git reads a file through a link the check never looked at. On Linux a share's text is a local path, so nothing leaves the machine there, and nothing was shown to run.
- The class, looked for in the two library files before the fix (PLAYBOOK "Testing": the class, not the example; line numbers of a1c7269, `plugins/trailmark/scripts/lib`). In it, each one answering `''` or passing the thing over on any failure. gitbin.js: 398 `localPath` (a failed `lstat` of a part of a path: the rest was kept as text and taken as local; RS-A-linkgit goes through it); 850 `unlisted`, with its callers at 888, 1348 and 1376 (a failed `readdir`, unless it was ENOENT or ENOTDIR with the folder still there, which gave `odd-path`; RS-A-bytepath); 559, 793, 919, 988, 1034 and 1333 (a `stat` after a link, or of an lfs folder, failed: "not a folder"); 1029 `realFolder`; 1044, the `readdir` in `otherWorktrees`; 1109, 1120 and 1131 in `farBareProbe`; 1159 and 1168 in `farGit` (the `.git` entry, and where a `.git` that is a link leads, which is RS-A-linkgit's line); 1290 in `farModulesIn`, and 1298, where an UNSAFE `commondir` was ignored; 1472 and 1489, the lookups on the way up in `farGitConfigIn`. gitfacts.js: 222 (a folder of tracked files, `continue`; RS-A-relpath), 250, 253, 266, 289, and 341 (`.lfsconfig`). Looked at and left, each with its reason. gitbin.js: 82 and 107 (finding git on PATH, no repo data); 304 `onDisk` (a failed realpath makes a folder be walked twice, never skipped); 421 `readSmall` and 517 `missingBase` (they already tell ENOENT and ENOTDIR from the rest, and were the model for the fix); 401 and 1114 (a failed readlink already refuses); 837 `headAt` and 842 `onlyFiles` (a failure makes the walk look at more, not less); 1004 `validGitdir.usable` and 1548 `localRepoRoot` (the root finder: RS-A-unreadroot, its own item); 1145, the branch of `farBareProbe` for a git before 2.38 (RS-A-oldgitprobe below). gitfacts.js: 225 (refuses), 495 `realOr` (falls back to comparing names), 625 and 774 (`missing-folder`, git not run).
- What a failed lookup says (`probe-codes.js`, 10:15, CONFIRMED here; `probe-codes-win.out`, `probe-codes-linux.out`). Windows, Node 26.13.1: each odd name tried gives ENOENT (a name of 255, 256, 300 and 5,000 letters; words with `|`, `*`, `?`, `<`, `>`, `"`, `:` or a tab; `con`, `nul`, `aux.txt`, `com1`; a name ending in a space or a dot; `Q:\x` and `A:\x` with no such drive). So the rule turned none of the alias values tried into a refusal there. EPERM for `C:\pagefile.sys`, `C:\hiberfil.sys` and `System32\config\SAM`, and for listing `C:\System Volume Information`, `C:\Documents and Settings` and `System32\config`. In a folder this user may not list (`icacls <folder> /deny <user>:(RD)`) a listing is EPERM, while a file in it, and one two levels in, is found and read by name. Linux (WSL, uid 1000): a name of 255 letters ENOENT; of 256, 300 and 5,000 ENAMETOOLONG; a path of 1,022, 1,023, 1,024 and 4,095 bytes ENOENT; of 4,096 ENAMETOOLONG; `/root/x` EACCES. A folder of mode 000: listing, lstat inside and read all EACCES. Mode 111: listing EACCES, a file in it found and read by name. Mode 444: it lists, lstat inside EACCES.
- The rule, and why. A lookup that fails says "not there" only when the system says so: ENOENT, ENOTDIR, or ENAMETOOLONG for a path of at most the bytes the system takes (then one name is longer than the file system holds, and nothing can be there by any route). Any other failure keeps git out, or, in the status check, skips the file list. The narrower ideas, and what each misses. Counting the cap of 4,096 in bytes outside Windows gives `long-path` for the two-byte shape, but not for a link whose text is short (RS-A-linkgit's link has 4,067 bytes of text), not at 4,096 bytes exactly, and not on macOS; the cap is about time and stays in characters. `odd-path` where the top joined to a tracked path is past the limit is the same rule at one place, with a constant where the lookup's own failure says it. Permissions: on Linux a lookup by name that fails with EACCES means a folder above can't be entered, and git as the same user can't pass it either. A failed listing is different (a folder of mode 0111 hides names git opens), and on Windows every user may pass through a folder they can't list. One rule for every call is simpler to check than a table of system, call and error, so every failure but "not there" refuses, with the one exception the next bullet gives.
- Fix, both copies. `gitbin.js`: `MAX_SYS_PATH` and `notThere(e, p)`, both exported. `MAX_SYS_PATH` is 4,095 on Linux and Android and 1,022 on any other system but Windows (two below the 1,024 of macOS's headers; HYPOTHESIZED until a Mac runs it). On Windows there is no limit in it: ENAMETOOLONG always counts as "not there" there, since git 2.56.1 opened nothing past about 260 characters when tried for RS-A-pathcap. `nothingIn(e, d)` is for a listing that failed: true for `notThere`, and outside Windows for EACCES when `access(d, X_OK)` fails with EACCES too. That is a folder nobody may enter, where no name opens by any path. The exception keeps the test "a decoy .git git can't search is passed over, as git does (loop round 4)" as it was: the first cut, without it, answered `unreadable-path` there on Linux (`wsl-suites-fix-1.out`, 10:33). A new reason `unreadable-path`. `localPath` hands back what it did before and sets a flag when it stops at a part it could not look at, so its callers outside the git checks get the answers they got (it is called from ten modules; a `null` there would have changed them and `localRepoRoot`). The entry points `farGitConfig`, `farNested`, `farModules` and `farLfsEntries` ask through `allSeen(fn)`, which turns an answer of `''` into `unreadable-path` when the flag was set, the way `limitedWalk` names `many-config-paths`. The sites of the class above answer `unreadable-path` for a failure that is not `notThere`, with three other words: `farLfsFile` and the status check's `.lfsconfig` answer `lfs-config`, an UNSAFE `commondir` in `farModulesIn` answers `unreadable-config`, and a listing goes through `nothingIn`. `gitfacts.js` also passes `unreadable-path` on from a nested check at the three places where another answer becomes `submodule-pointer`. `localRepoRoot` is not changed.
- With the fix (`repro-fix-1.out`, WSL, 10:29, before `nothingIn` was added; CONFIRMED here): each shape of the three probes that answered `''` on a1c7269 answers `unreadable-path`; the short controls and the `long-path` shapes are as before. The probes were not run again after `nothingIn`; the on-disk tests below build the same three shapes and ran after it.
- Changes in behavior for ordinary repos. Git is kept out (`unreadable-path`) where a folder inside `.git`, an `lfs.storage` folder or a store next to an alternate can't be listed: outside Windows one that can be entered and not listed, on Windows any listing that fails. Outside Windows also (taken back in review round 1, below: `''` again) where a setting names a file below a folder that can't be entered (`core.excludesFile` under a folder of mode 0000, and `/root/.gitignore_global` as uid 1000: `''` before, in `probe-root-2.out`), and on Linux in a session folder at 4,091 bytes and up inside a repo, where the `.git` looked for is past 4,095 bytes and git itself stops (next bullet). The file list is skipped for a tracked path that is past the system's limit once joined to the top, and for a folder of tracked files that can't be looked at. Windows, by reasoning from `probe-deny.js` (10:27) and not run as a session: a lookup by name fails with EPERM only where the entry denies the user on itself and its folder may not be listed, so a repo behind two such levels gets `unreadable-path`. macOS: a session folder at about 1,019 bytes and up, by the model below (HYPOTHESIZED). Not changed: a folder this user may not enter; one name over 255 bytes at a path within the limit (ENAMETOOLONG, still "not there"); the callers of `localPath` outside the git checks; `localRepoRoot`.
- The root (`probe-root.js`, WSL, 11:08, `probe-root-2.out`: a1c7269's two library files against the fix's, 18 shapes; CONFIRMED here). `localRepoRoot` answers the same in all 18. The root a session gets moved in 5 of them. First move: a session folder inside a repo at 4,091 and at 4,095 bytes (git stops there with "fatal: error reading" its `.git`, exit 128) and at 4,096 bytes (git can't be started, ENAMETOOLONG). The check let git run before and git failed, so the root was the session's own folder; it is the repo above now, found without git. At 4,090 bytes nothing changes, and at 4,097 it is `long-path` before and after. Second move: a folder below one whose `.git` is a link to a gitdir at 4,096 bytes, with a plain config and with one that includes a share. Git answered the folder with the link; `localRepoRoot` finds nothing there (`''`), so the root is the session's own folder now. ## RS-A-pathcap round 1 (2026-11-13, reviewed on d61366c; the batch is the next commit)

Three reviewers in detached clones under `E:/DevTemp`, on `git diff cf2c007..d61366c`: security (Fable), regression (Opus), docs (Sonnet). Their reports are in the notes file `rs-a-pathcap-longname-notes.md`, sections "Round 1". Each finding acted on was reproduced here first, in fresh processes with three sets of scripts (cf2c007, d61366c, the batch). The scripts named are in the session's scratch folder, with a copy in `rs-a-pathcap-scripts/`. No reviewer had an access finding, and nothing was shown to run or leak.

- Wrong in d61366c, CONFIRMED here: the cap changed which folder is taken for the repo's root, and so the memory folder. `repoRoot` (`paths.js`) asks `farGitConfig` first, and on a refusal takes the root from `localRepoRoot` and no longer from git. The regression reviewer's finding, Windows: a session folder inside a repo that is a junction to a path past the cap (237 characters as given, 4,097 where it leads). git 2.56.1 works there (`rev-parse --show-toplevel` gives the repo, `status --short` exits 0). cf2c007 answered `''` with root the repo; d61366c `long-path` with root the session folder. On Linux (WSL) `git rev-parse` fails to stat in such a folder and the roots were equal. Then mine, the reverse, where git fails: a session folder given at 4,097 or 4,200 characters in a repo at a short path; a `.git` file naming a gitdir at 4,097 characters; a gitdir whose `commondir` names a folder at 4,097; a repo at the end of a junction whose `.git` leads to 4,096 or 4,097; on Linux a link leading into a repo and to 4,097 bytes. In each, cf2c007's root was the session folder and d61366c's a repo above it. Scripts: `probe-linkedcwd.js` (outputs `-1` to `-6` and `-linux-2`), `probe-given.js`, `probe-under.js`, `probe-commoncap.js`.
- The time, CONFIRMED here (`measure-root.js`): `repoRoot` as a whole for a session folder 15,000 folders down (30,022 characters) took 14.6 to 15.4 s on cf2c007 and 7.4 to 7.5 s on d61366c. The check answered at once, and `localRepoRoot` then walked the same path with no look at the time. At 8,000 characters 1.6 to 1.7 s and 0.7 to 0.9 s; at 4,098 0.56 to 0.58 s and 0.25 to 0.26 s. The security reviewer's finding 3 is the same (7.39 to 7.45 s). The first notes' "0.00 to 0.15 s" was the check alone.
- The security reviewer's finding 5, CONFIRMED here (`probe-fable.js`): `farModules` called alone, for a `.git` file naming a gitdir at 4,097 characters that holds `modules/m` with a commondir on a share, answered `network-gitdir` on cf2c007 and `''` on d61366c: the `long-path` of the `farGit` that finds the gitdir was dropped. In the hook `farGitConfig` is asked first and answers `long-path` (CONFIRMED by the reviewer by reading, not re-run).
- The security reviewer's finding 1, CONFIRMED here (`probe-fable.js --mod`), older code that d61366c's new SECURITY.md sentence did not cover: the walk for submodule gitdirs had no cap. A submodule gitdir's `annex` with 10,001 files, then a folder chained down to 15,000 characters that holds 30,000 empty folders: `farModules` took 7.62 to 7.70 s with 30,044 listings past the cap, on cf2c007 and on d61366c.
- The fix, `gitbin.js`, both copies. The rule: the cap never changes the root (too wide: see round 2 below). (A) `farGitConfigIn` caps where the session folder's links lead outside Windows only. (B) `localRepoRoot` answers `''` at once for a folder given past the cap, and outside Windows for one whose links lead past it: git can't be started there, and the root was the folder itself. (C) On Windows `localRepoRoot` gives no root at a `.git` whose gitdir, or the `objects` folder of its gitdir or commondir, is past the cap: git stopped with an error there, and the root was the session folder. (D) `farModulesIn` passes `long-path` on. (E) `moduleGitdirs` lists no folder past the cap, in its walk and in `objects`.
- (C) was first written for every system, from probes run on Windows. The Linux run of the tests (23:39, after the first whole mutation list) failed, and `probe-under.js` showed that the batch had moved the root on Linux for a commondir at 4,095, 4,096 and 4,097 characters: the repo above on cf2c007, the session folder on the batch. Outside Windows nothing at such a path could be read before the cap either (`unreadable-config`), so git was already kept out and the root already came from `localRepoRoot`. With (C) on Windows only, `probe-under.js` gives cf2c007's root in 16 of 16 cases (a `.git` file's gitdir and a commondir, at 4,000, 4,095, 4,096 and 4,097 characters, on Windows and in WSL; `probe-under-2.out`, 23:42), and `probe-given.js` in 10 of 10 (a session folder as text at five lengths, both systems, 23:41, before that last change: its lines are not in (C)).
- With the fix, CONFIRMED here: the junction shape answers `''` with root the repo again; each shape where git fails has cf2c007's root; `repoRoot` for the folder 15,000 down takes 6 to 7 ms and at 8,000 characters 2 to 3 ms, and at 4,096, which is let through, 0.55 to 0.65 s on all three; finding 5's shape answers `long-path`; finding 1's shape answers `long-path` in 0.01 s with 0 listings. The price of (A) on Windows: a session folder given at 4,096 characters through a junction leading to 7,955 takes the check 0.83 to 0.96 s (`deep-folder`), as on cf2c007 (0.83 to 0.92 s; d61366c 0.58 s); with no link 0.31 to 0.38 s (`measure-linkedcwd.js`). The timings of this paragraph are from before (C) went to Windows only; that line is not on their way.

## RS-A-pathcap round 2 (2026-11-14, reviewed on ba33ffd; the batch is the next commit)

Three reviewers in detached clones under `E:/DevTemp`, on `git diff d61366c..ba33ffd`: security (Fable), regression (Opus), docs (Sonnet). Their reports are in the notes file `rs-a-pathcap-longname-notes.md`, sections "Round 2". Each finding acted on was reproduced here first, with three sets of scripts in fresh processes (cf2c007, d61366c, ba33ffd or the batch). No serious finding: nothing was shown to run or leak. Not clean: round 1's rule "the cap never changes the root" is false, in lines ba33ffd changed and in d61366c's. The batch changes no line of code. It says what holds in SECURITY.md, in the comments and here, and defers what is older.

- Why the rule can't hold, CONFIRMED here: where git gives no answer, cf2c007's root was the session's folder when git was let try, and `localRepoRoot`'s answer when git was kept out (`repoRoot`, `paths.js`). For a folder past the cap, telling the two apart needs the walk the cap is there to avoid (8.3 to 8.5 s for a folder 15,000 down). ba33ffd gives cf2c007's answer for the first case, the one with no other reason to keep git out. d61366c gave it for the second and took 7.5 s.
- The security reviewer's finding 1, CONFIRMED here (`probe-secroots.js`, Windows 00:58 and WSL 00:58), in ba33ffd's lines (B) and (C): where cf2c007 already kept git out for another reason, the root moved from the repo to the session's folder. A folder at 4,097 characters inside `R/.git/x`: `inside-gitdir` on all three, root R on cf2c007 and d61366c, the folder itself on ba33ffd (both systems). A folder at 4,097 in a repo whose config includes `//evil.invalid/share/x`: cf2c007 `network-config` root R; ba33ffd `long-path` root the folder (both systems); with a plain config cf2c007's root is the folder too. On Linux the same through a link that leads to that folder. On Windows, a `.git` file in W naming a valid gitdir at 4,097 with that include, session in `W/sub`: cf2c007 `unreadable-config` root W; ba33ffd root `W/sub`; with a plain config cf2c007's root is `W/sub` too.
- The security reviewer's finding 2 and the regression reviewer's finding 2, CONFIRMED here (`probe-secroots.js`, `probe-roots2.js`), Windows, from d61366c on: where Git for Windows fails for a reason of its own and the cap now keeps it out for something else in the repo, the root moved from the session's folder to the repo. A repo at 300 characters with a folder inside `.git` at about 4,100, session in `R/s`: git can't be started (ENOENT); cf2c007 `''` root `R/s`; d61366c and ba33ffd `long-path` root R. The same repo at 3,900 characters through a junction: git exits 128 ("Filename too long"), cf2c007's root is the session's folder, now the repo. A repo R at a short path with a stale alternate that names a path of 4,200 characters, session folder at 300 characters: cf2c007 root the session's folder, now R. In WSL the roots are equal (the reviewer's run, and `probe-secroots.js` has no such case there).
- The regression reviewer's finding 1, CONFIRMED here (`probe-roots2.js` case "s1 long", 00:14): repo A with a junction into a folder of repo B at about 500 characters and the same stale alternate in A. git answers A. cf2c007 `''` root A; d61366c and ba33ffd `long-path` root B. With the junction's target at a short path git itself answers B and all three agree, which is why my first run (00:11) did not show it. `probe-getcwd.js`: git goes by where the links lead up to a real path of 250 characters and by the path as given from 256.
- These roots are not new ones: with a reason that predates the cap (an alternate on a share, `network-config`), cf2c007 gives root B in the junction shape and root R for the folder at 300 characters (`probe-roots2-3.out`, 00:18). So the cap adds repos that reach `localRepoRoot`; it does not make `localRepoRoot` answer anything it did not answer before, except `''` for a folder or a gitdir past the cap.
- What the batch changes: SECURITY.md's `long-path` bullet is three bullets; the third says where the root comes from and each case above. The comments in `gitbin.js` (the cap in `farGitConfigIn`, `localRepoRoot`'s header and its two checks) and the test's comment no longer say "never"; `edit-round2-comments.js` refuses a change to a line that is not a comment. MANUAL.md's `long-path` row: what to do for a link, an alternate or `lfs.storage`, and "through a junction to a path of 256 characters or more". ## Next version: RS-A-dotpath (2026-11-13, branch `claude/rs-a-dotpath` off 6cfb0e0, merged in PR #57 as 318223d)

The user pulled it in ("Yes, fix next", 2026-11-13). Fable found it in round 1 of RS-A-redirect; it is older than that PR.

- The hole (CONFIRMED here on 6cfb0e0, `probe-dslash.js`, 17:12, git 2.56.1 on Windows): an index written by hand that names a tracked file `d//b.bin`, `d/./b.bin` or `d///b.bin`, with a line of the same text in `.git/info/attributes` that gives it a filter of the repo's own config. `git check-attr` answered `unspecified` for the path, so `filterOverrides` left the filter on, and `git status` ran it during `gitFacts(dir, ['status'])`. The control `d/b.bin` was switched off. On Linux (WSL, git 2.56.1) the real-repos test below fails on 6cfb0e0's `gitfacts.js` at `d//b.bin` (CONFIRMED here, 17:37).
- What raw git does (CONFIRMED here, git 2.56.1 on Windows). `probe-dotpath2.js` (17:14, kept as `probe-dotpath2-win.txt`): `git update-index --add --cacheinfo` refuses `d//c`, `d/./c`, `./c`, `c/`, `d/.` and `.` with "Invalid path". From an index written by hand, the filter ran for `d//b.bin`, `d/./b.bin` and `./d/b.bin` (check-attr said `unspecified` each time), and did not run for `d/b.bin/`, `d/.` and `.`. An entry with no name is listed as `./`. With a sparse index, `git ls-files --stage` without `--sparse` lists the files, and no entry ends in a slash. `probe-dotpath3.js` (17:26, kept as `probe-dotpath3-win.txt`): `git add` with `d//f`, `d/./f`, `./d/f` or `d///f` wrote `d/f`; a tree built by hand with an entry named `.` was refused by `git read-tree` and by `git checkout -f` ("invalid path 'd/./b.bin'"), and one with an entry with no name by both and by `git ls-tree -r` ("empty filename in tree entry"); the index was empty after each.
- That git's own commands never give a tracked file such a path was INFERRED from those routes, which all had a full index. RULED OUT for a sparse index in round 2: `git checkout` took a tree with such a part in a folder outside the cone, and git then failed to list the files, so status stayed unread (section "RS-A-dotpath round 2"). With a full index it stays INFERRED. Other programs that write an index (libgit2, JGit, dulwich, gitoxide) were not tried: none is installed here, and trying one needs a download. If one of them writes such a path, the snapshot says `not read (odd-path)` for that repo and nothing else changes (HYPOTHESIZED that none does).
- Fix: one check in `farWorktree` (`scripts/lib/gitfacts.js`, both copies). A tracked path with an empty part or a part of one dot gives `odd-path`, and status is not read. The parts are split at `/` only: a backslash is a character of a name on Linux and macOS, and Windows refuses any backslash by the older rule. One place, since `gitFacts` asks `farWorktree` first and `filterOverrides` only when it found nothing.
- Tests, two, in both copies. A decision test with git stood in for: an empty part and a part of one dot, put in at every place of three paths and in place of each of their parts (29 shapes) and 8 more shapes with two or three such parts, each alone and as the first, the middle and the last of three; a part of two dots, refused as before; parts with dots that are taken; backslashes and parts of three or more dots, taken on Linux and macOS. A real-repos test with an index written by hand: six names, each gives `odd-path`. For four of them (`d//b.bin`, `d/./b.bin`, `d///b.bin`, `./d/b.bin`) the case also says the filter's marker is absent, then asks git itself for status and requires the marker, so each of those cases shows the filter would have run. The other two (`d/b.bin/`, `d/.`) say only that status is not read, since git did not run the filter for them. `d/b.bin` is the control: switched off, and git itself then runs the filter.
- The first form of the real-repos test said the marker was absent for all six names. Two of them could not have written it (PLAYBOOK "Testing" step 8), so the test was changed before the commit, and every run below is on the changed test.
- Checked here on this tree (CONFIRMED). Mutation list (`mutate-dotpath.js`, 21 entries with the unchanged file last, each through `dev/release-check.sh --only 'RS-A-dotpath'`, kept as `mutate-dotpath-2.txt`, 17:35:00 to 17:37:25): the code before the fix and 17 changes to the fix each fail as listed before the run (16 entries fail all 4, 2 fail 2 of 4), the two changes listed as passing on Windows pass, and the unchanged file passes 4 of 4. With `[filter "set"]` (or one of the other three names) and a `clean` command in the repo's own `.git/config`, the status call got no `-c filter.<name>.clean=` and the command ran when a hook read `git status`. The same line is in v0.5.0 and v0.6.2. What it needs: a folder that came with its own `.git/config` (an unpacked archive, a copied folder); a clone does not carry one.
- The class (PLAYBOOK "Writing code and docs" step 11): a text from git that stands for two things. By grep over `scripts/` in both copies:
  - `filterOverrides` is the only place that reads values of `check-attr`, and `gitFacts` (one call, for `status`) is its only caller.
  - `git status` is the only git command the code runs that runs filters.
  - The four texts are the whole list of what git prints for an attribute that has no value of its own (git's page on `check-attr`, read here in the installed copy: `unspecified`, `unset`, `set`, else the value; that a value may be empty is from the probe, `*.bin filter=`). The page itself ends its examples with "Not all values are equally unambiguous" and an attribute whose value is the word `unspecified`.

If any, one more call (`git config -z --get-regexp '^filter\.(set|unset|unspecified)?\.'`) lists the settings of filters under the four names in every config git reads. A setting of a filter whose name is one of the texts seen gives `odd-filter-name`, and status is not read. Exit status 1 from the call means no such setting. Any other failure gives `filter-check`, or `git-timeout` for a timeout. `filterOverrides` is exported, for its test.
- What that costs a user: a filter so named in the user's own global or system config skips status too (the call does not ask for scopes), and a filter named `unspecified` does it in nearly every repo, since nearly every repo has a file with no filter. Renaming the filter brings status back. Kept this way on purpose: telling the scopes apart would leave the repo's own filter of that name to be found by a second rule, and no tool known here names a filter so (INFERRED: Git LFS uses `lfs`, and git's page on attributes uses `indent`, `crypt` and `p4`, read here in the installed copy; not searched further).

## Next version: RS-A-deepindex (2026-11-12, branch `claude/rs-a-deepindex` off 4299c47, merged in PR #53 as 5a15974)

PR #52 (RS-A-worktreeslinks) merged as 4299c47 at 2026-11-12 07:23:56Z, through auto-merge, with 9 of 9 jobs passed on its last head 8110e55 (CONFIRMED here from `gh pr view`). It merged under the user's delegation of 2026-11-11 (a deferred item's PR merges once its review round is clean and the checks pass): round 6 (Sonnet, docs, on dac303c..8110e55, a test comment and these notes only) found nothing wrong (CONFIRMED by Sonnet, not re-run). The merge command was a step of its own, after the pushed head showed its 9 jobs. Round 6's two points that could be clearer, not changed: the test comment's "more than 4% of what an entry counts" stands next to "a cut-off below about 15,400 characters" without saying the 4% is of an entry's count of about 19,240; and the notes could say once that 96% is the worktrees check's own share and 97% the whole check's.

- What was wrong, CONFIRMED here on 4299c47 (Windows, Node 26.13.1, git 2.56.1, `measure-deepindex.js`, three runs each, a library timing): `farWorktree` in `gitfacts.js` built `parts.slice(0, i).join('/')` for every level of every tracked path and looked it up in a Set, and nothing in that loop looked at the time. The work grows with the files times the square of the depth. Only an index is needed (`git update-index --index-info`, nothing checked out): with 1,500 files in one folder 1,500 deep, `gitFacts(r, ['status'], { budgetMs: 5000 })` took 12.18 to 12.24 s and answered `git-timeout`; 500 files 1,000 deep took 2.44 to 2.46 s; 500 files 1,000 deep, each in a last folder of its own, 2.54 s.
- Through the real PreCompact hook (`time-deepindex-hook.js`: the launcher started as a process with a home folder of its own, in a repo set up with `trailmark.js init --force`, parent and fix in turn, CONFIRMED here): 1,500 files 1,500 deep took 14.45 and 14.93 s on 4299c47, past the 10 s at which Claude Code stops a hook, and 1.53 and 1.47 s with the fix; 500 files 1,000 deep 3.01 and 2.88 s against 1.06 and 1.10 s; a repo with nothing tracked 0.86 to 0.92 s on both.
- On Linux (WSL Ubuntu, Node 18.19.1, git 2.56.1, the same library script, parent, fix, fix, parent, three runs each, CONFIRMED here): 1,500 files 1,500 deep took 26.86 to 28.55 s on 4299c47 (`git-timeout`) and 0.38 to 0.40 s with the fix, 1,500 counted. macOS is not timed; CI runs the test there.
- Fix, `gitfacts.js`, both copies:
  - The folders are kept as a tree of names (`tree = { path, kids: Map }`). Each level of a path costs one `kids.get` of that level's name, and a path string is built only when a folder is new. The list `folders` is an array filled in the same order as before (a folder after its parents), and `folders.length >= MAX_TREE_FOLDERS` answers `many-folders` as before. The work now follows the size of git's list, whatever its order.
  - The loop looks at the time once for each `LIST_STEP` (1,048,576) characters of git's list and answers `git-timeout` with under 800 ms left, the same floor as the loops after it. A list can be 32 MB (`maxBuffer`), so that is at most 32 looks; a list more than one character under 1 MB gets none (corrected in round 1: the empty piece after the last NUL counts 1).
  - `farWorktree` is exported for its test.
- With the fix (same script, three runs each, CONFIRMED here): the three shapes above take 1.08 to 1.11 s, 0.76 to 0.80 s and 0.84 to 0.98 s, with the right count each time. Larger: 100,000 files 20 deep 1.23 to 1.24 s; 19,900 files 100 deep, each in a folder of its own, 2.19 to 2.25 s; 5,000 files 3,000 deep (a list of 30 MB) 2.50 to 2.60 s, answer `git-error`.
- That `git-error` is `git status` itself, CONFIRMED here (`probe-deepindex-giterror.js`): with tracked paths of 4,122 characters or more, Git for Windows 2.56.1 stops with `BUG: compat/win32/fscache.c:133: Trying to allocate fsentry for long path` (exit 3221226505), and with 4,082 it answers. `rev-parse` and both `ls-files` calls answer at 6,002 characters. Status is left out with a word, as for any other git error. Not looked at: what git on Linux or macOS does with such paths.
- One very long path (`probe-deepindex-shapes.js`, a made-up `r`, CONFIRMED here): one tracked path of 16 MB with 19,000 folders ran node out of memory on 4299c47 (the old loop joins 19,000 paths of 8 MB on average). With the fix the list is gone through, and the loop over the folders, which looks at the time before each one, answers `git-timeout` after 4.20 to 4.22 s of the 5 s given, with 76 to 182 MB in use. Names of 20 and of 100 characters at that depth give the same answer after 4.20 s. The fix adds a folder's name to its parent's path, and node keeps such a text as its two parts until it is used, so no whole path is built in the first loop; the test holds that by the memory in use. One path of 16 MB with 8,000,000 folders answers `many-folders` in 0.31 to 0.32 s (2.13 and 2.55 s on 4299c47).
- The class, by reading every step between `ls-files` and `git status` (lesson "A fix covered the reviewer's example, not its class"): the first loop's other work for an entry follows the entry's length, and now has the look at the time; the loop that fills `byFolder` does two Map lookups (`has` and `get`, corrected in round 1) of the folder's whole path for each entry and has no look; the `byFolder` loop looks every 500 folders; the `folders` loop looks before each folder; `filterOverrides` follows the list and runs git under timeouts. No other step was found whose work grows faster than the list. The loop without a look is covered by the 30 MB run above for a list of many entries: the whole call took 2.50 to 2.60 s, git included. (Corrected in round 1: it is not covered for one name of 30 MB, RS-A-longname below.)
- Test, `handoff-checks.test.js`, both copies: "git status: finding the folders of tracked files takes work that follows the list, and looks at the time (RS-A-deepindex)". It hands `farWorktree` a made-up `r` (`run` answers `rev-parse` and `ls-files` from a list built in the test, `left` is scripted and counted) and counts work, not seconds: the characters of every string key looked up in a Map or Set during the call. Cases: the folders are looked at in the order `a`, `a/b`, `a/b/c`, `a/x`, `z`; 200 files 400 deep look up less than 8 times the list's length and more than once (the fix: 399,600 characters for a list of 170,890, 2.34 times; the old loop: 32,319,600, 189 times); a list of 2.6 MB in one folder asks for the time 3 times and passes; with the second ask at 500 ms the answer is `git-timeout` after 2 asks and no folder is looked at; with it at 800 the answer is `''`; a short list asks once; 20,001 folders answer `many-folders` with no folder looked at; one path 1,500 folders deep with names of 400 characters (a list of 600,000 characters, whose folders' paths add up to 450 MB) grows the memory in use by less than 100 times the list before the first look at the time.
- The test fails on 4299c47 only because `farWorktree` is not exported there (a TypeError), which proves nothing about the fix. The proof is the mutation that puts the old loop back in the new file: it fails 2 of 2.
- Mutations (`mutate-deepindex.js`, each through `dev/release-check.sh --only 'RS-A-deepindex'`, 14 probes, one whole run after the last case was added, CONFIRMED here): 13 caught 2 of 2 and the unchanged fix passes. Caught: the old loop back; no look at the time; a look for every entry; a look for each 1,048,576 entries in place of characters; `LIST_STEP` 100 times larger; `LIST_STEP` half as large; the floor at 250 ms; the floor at 900 ms; a new folder's path without its parent; a new folder's whole path joined from its parts (`parts.slice(0, i + 1).join('/')`, which only the memory case tells); no limit on the folders; the file's own name taken for a folder; `gitfacts.js` of 4299c47.
- No shipped doc changes. MANUAL.md, SECURITY.md and docs/how-it-works.md name `many-folders` and `git-timeout` and say nothing about this loop or its time (checked by grep), and the answers are unchanged. CHANGELOG.md gets its lines at the release step, as for the earlier deferred items.
- Not shown: a time on macOS. Not settled, and not worth its cost: whether git accepts an index whose entries are out of order (INFERRED: it checks the order only in `fsck`). Making one means writing the index file by hand, and the answer changes nothing: the tree's work does not depend on the order, and the test's first case hands the entries over out of order.
- Lesson logged: "A hook timing read the same on the old code and the fix, because the hook had left early".

Fix idea: a limit of about 20 minutes per job, in a PR of its own. Repro: the run above. Worked on 2026-11-15 in section "Next version: RS-D-jobtimeout", with limits per system (healthy Windows jobs took up to 21.5 minutes, so 20 would have cancelled them).

- What was wrong, CONFIRMED here on 60c2a4b (Windows): the first thing a hook does is find the repo's memory folder (`hookMemory` in the launcher, then `findMemoryDir` and `repoRoot` in `lib/paths.js`), and `repoRoot` ran the check of the repo's config files with no look at the hook's time. The hook's 5 s for git were counted from the hook's start, so this check's cost came off what `gitFacts` got afterwards, but nothing stopped the check itself. Through the real PreCompact hook (`repro-nestedone-hook.js`, the launcher started as a process and timed from outside): with the session 8 folders down, each folder with a `.git` whose config includes 20 files with a quote, the hook takes 12.3 to 13.5 s today (four rounds of three hooks; 10.05 to 10.30 s when RS-A-nestedone measured it); with no includes 0.87 to 0.96 s. The same check had no limit in the context watch, which runs after every tool call past its first step, in the PreToolUse hook, which Claude Code and Codex stop after 5 s, and in the sweep's lookup of each folder the session committed in.
- Fix:
  - `lib/paths.js`, both copies (the same text but for two comment lines): `repoRoot(cwd, timeoutMs, left)` takes what is left of the caller's time as a function. With it, the check and each git call run inside `withTime(left, fn, 250)`; no git call is started with under 250 ms left; and a git call's timeout is what is left, in whole ms, up to its own (`timeoutMs`). A check that ran out of time, a git call not started and a git call that timed out all end the same way: the root is found from the `.git` entries (`localRepoRoot`), with no git and no config file read. The check `git()` makes right before it starts git answers out of time as a timeout too. `findMemoryDir` hands on `ctx.left`. With no `left` nothing changes. One command does hand a clock in: `write-handoff` with `--session`, through its sweep (round 1).
  - The launchers, each by hand: `hookMemory` takes the clock and gives it to both lookups, the one from the hook's folder and the one from the folder the session started in. `hookMode` hands in 5 s less the time since the hook started, and 3 s for the PreToolUse hook. The sweep's lookup gets its deadline less the 0.8 s it already kept back. Claude Code's copy: the context watch hands in the same 5 s.
  - A decision: the PreToolUse hook names 3 s, not 5. Both hosts stop that hook after 5 s, it holds up the user's command, and it still has to start the writer for its record (a plain hook takes 0.9 s here). With 5 s the check could run for 4.75 s and the record would be lost to the host's limit, as it was before the fix.
- After, CONFIRMED here: the same real hook takes 4.92 to 4.99 s; two nested gitdirs 4.45 s (4.4 s before); no includes 0.90 to 0.95 s. The snapshot then says "Uncommitted files: not read (git-timeout)", since the first check used the 5 s: the hook is on time and says what it couldn't read. The old and the new code were timed in turn (old, new, new, old, three hooks each time; the old code from `git archive 60c2a4b` in a folder of its own).
- A change in behavior: a hook whose first check takes longer than its time now finds the memory folder without git and reads no status. Before, it went on until the host stopped it (10 s, 15 s for PreCompact; 5 s for PreToolUse), and a hook that was stopped wrote nothing.
- Tests:
  - "git pointers: finding the repo for a hook stops with the hook's time (RS-A-firstcheck)", `handoff-checks.test.js`, both copies. Part 1, the two libraries loaded afresh for each case, with stand-ins that note the timeout of each git call and the line each `withTime` call names, and that run every call with 20 s: no clock, and a number in place of one, as before; 5 s, 2000.7 ms, 2 s with git calls of 1 s, NaN, Infinity; 250 ms goes on and 249 ms reads no file and starts no git, and the root is still the repo; short of time from the third file; short after the check; rev-parse stopped; the first rev-parse failing and the second one's time; out of time in the check before git; git kept out; and `findMemoryDir` handing the time on. The cost: a repo on Windows whose index holds such a name (one that can't be checked out there with git's defaults) gets no file list in its snapshot.
